newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: OECD sees South Korea's membership as bridge to Asia.
newsitem.headline: OECD sees South Korea's membership as bridge to Asia.

text.p: South Korea's planned entry to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) will serve as a bridge between Asia and the developed world, a top OECD official said on Thursday.
OECD Secretary-General Donald Johnston told a seminar in Seoul that South Korea would be the group's second member from Asia after Japan.
"Korea's extensive economic relations with major economies in the region, including China, situate it well to perform as an OECD bridge to the Asia-Pacific," he said.

Johnston said Seoul could assist not only in integrating China and other Asian nations into the global economy, but also in the "strengthening of democratic institutions and the observance of human rights" in the region.
South Korea's parliament this week ratified the country's OECD membership, removing the last hurdle to joining the club of established economies.
Seoul officials said President Kim Young-sam would soon sign the membership agreement, expanding the OECD to 29 countries and giving the Paris-based club greater weight in Asia.

Johnston told reporters later that no other Asian countries were considered as a new OECD member in the near future but the group's cooperation was "bound to be reinforced in Asia" because of dynamic economic growth in the region.
"So it's clear that Korea will play a very important role in shaping those relationships," he told a news conference.

Seoul was invited to join the OECD on October 11, but members of the opposition had threatened to block ratification in parliament, saying the OECD could force South Korea to open its local markets to foreign competition too quickly.
Since applying for OECD membership in March 1995, South Korea has accelerated the opening of its financial markets to foreign investors and pledged further reforms.
Johnston said South Korea's liberalisation policy was in the country's own interest.
"The greatest economic policy challenge facing Korea may indeed be the completion of the liberalisation process begun in the early 1980s," he said.

The reduction of the average tariff rate from more than 40 percent in 1978 to six percent in 1994, the decision to abolish all but eight import quotas by July 1997, less interventionist industrial and financial policies, all contributed to rapid economic growth, he said.
"Taking further steps to remove controls on capital flows should help reduce interest rates in Korea, which remain six to seven points above the rates seen in international markets."

South Korea's main opposition National Congress for New Politics has said the rapid opening of the financial markets could deal a blow to the economy, already suffering from a growing trade deficit and inflationary pressures.
The government projects the nation's current account deficit will rise to about $20 billion in calendar 1996 from a shortfall of $8.9 billion in 1995.
William Witherell, OECD director in charge of financial affairs, dismissed as unwarranted worries that Seoul could face an economic crisis like Mexico did after it joined the OECD in 1994.
"I really wouldn't expect the Mexican experience to be repeated here," Witherell told reporters.
He said unlike Mexico's rapid removal of controls on foreign exchange and short-term capital flows, South Korea was committed to phased capital market liberalisation over a number of years.
